corrections.source_says: The three criterion fields are blank. Under the supplied codebook, record not_met, met, and not_met, respectively: the study is observational, the corpus represents 2000 unique students, and the scored outcomes concern style, sentiment, and academic quality rather than creativity or diversity across different writers. The existing core = no and context_class = none are supported.
corrections.quote: the observational nature of this study prevents us from concluding that these changes were causally driven by GenAI.
corrections.locator: PDF p. 2, Section 1.3; pp. 3-4, Sections 2.5-2.8; p. 12, Sections 4.5 and 5; creativity-codebook.md, Sections 3 and 6

corrections.source_says: Use none for S1-O1 through S1-O4. These are within-report vocabulary variety, lexical markers of possible AI use, sentiment, and academic grades; they do not answer the atlas questions about creativity with AI, diversity across people, or creativity after AI removal. AI availability by calendar period does not make these measures qualifying creativity outcomes.
corrections.quote: We used Measure of Textual Lexical Diversity (MTLD; McCarthy & Jarvis, 2010) to capture the range of unique words in a text while controlling for text length.
corrections.locator: PDF pp. 3-4, Sections 2.5-2.8; p. 12, Sections 4.5 and 5; form-spec.md, question field note; creativity-codebook.md, Sections 1 and 6

confirmed: Independently read the complete 19-page journal version of record in memory from https://wrap.warwick.ac.uk/id/eprint/195006/1/1-s2.0-S2666920X2500147X-main.pdf, including Appendices 1-8 and references. The title and both authors match the form; the document identifies Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence 9 (2025), 100507, received 9 October 2025, accepted 24 November 2025, and available online 26 November 2025 (PDF p. 1; appendices pp. 13-18). No local markdown or PDF is supplied by retrieval.json.

No randomized people study is reported. S1 is an observational comparison of coursework submitted before and after ChatGPT; S2 compares GPT rewrites of existing reports with their originals, without assigning students to receive AI. The five informal student interviews informed the rewriting prompt and were not an experiment (PDF p. 2, Section 1.3; pp. 3-5, Methods and Sections 2.9-2.10).

The corpus contains 4820 reports by 2000 unique psychology undergraduates, with 17.2 million word tokens; 3033 reports are pre-ChatGPT and 1787 are post-ChatGPT. Special Cohorts 1 and 2 contain 155 and 164 students, respectively. These are corpus/cohort counts, not randomized-arm counts; the student corpus exceeds 50 people (PDF p. 2, Section 1.3; p. 3, Section 2.4; p. 17, Appendix 6; p. 18, Appendix 8).

S2 uses 3033 pre-ChatGPT reports, not 3033 randomized people. GPT-3.5-Turbo version 0125 and GPT-4o mini version 2024-07-18 rewrote the reports sentence by sentence at temperature 0.7; the respective rewritten corpora contain 11.3 and 9.6 million tokens, versus 10.9 million in the originals. A separate unique-person count for this subset is not stated (PDF pp. 4-5, Section 2.9).

The observational design classification and exclusion from both core and eligible context evidence are supported under the supplied codebook: MTLD measures vocabulary variety within a text, and creativity/epistemic diversity are proposed for future study. There is no measure of diversity across writers in this paper (PDF pp. 3-4, Sections 2.5-2.8; p. 12, Sections 4.5 and 5).

S1-O1 reported statistics match the PDF: 2025 actual 84.71 [83.30, 86.13] vs predicted 72.98 [71.68, 74.28], difference +11.73; Post-ChatGPT trend B = 7.115, SE = 0.345, t = 20.617, p < 0.001 (PDF p. 13, Appendix 1, Lexical Diversity).

S1-O2 reported statistics match the PDF: In 2024, prevalence exploded to 0.226 ... exceeding the 95 % confidence intervals of the projected trend [0.035, 0.181]; in 2025 prevalence declined by 17.2 % (vs. 2024) to 0.188, just below the upper bound of the projected trend [0.039, 0.193] (PDF p. 5, Section 3.1).

S1-O3 reported statistics match the PDF, including the SE rounded to 0.000: 2025 actual 0.0450 [0.0438, 0.0462] vs predicted 0.0357 [0.0339, 0.0374], difference +0.0093; Post-ChatGPT trend B = 0.002, SE = 0.000, t = 4.477, p < 0.001 (PDF p. 14, Appendix 1, Sentiment).

S1-O4 reported statistics match the PDF: 2025 actual 64.23 [63.49, 64.96] vs predicted 64.26 [63.08, 65.40], difference −0.03; Post-ChatGPT trend B = 0.103, SE = 0.293, t = 0.352, p = 0.725 (PDF p. 14, Appendix 1, Score; p. 10, Section 3.4).

S2-O1 reported means match the PDF: MGPT-3.5 = 0.453 for, MGPT-4o-mini = 0.447, compared to the pre-ChatGPT student originals (M = 0.069). The incidental word for after 0.453 is printed in the source. The sentiment comparison ps < 0.001, ds > 0.77 in measure_detail also matches (PDF p. 5, Section 3.1; p. 9, Section 3.3).
All numbers in one_line_finding match their cited passages; the grade result is a nonsignificant post-ChatGPT trend with p = 0.725 (PDF p. 5, Section 3.1; pp. 13-14, Appendix 1).
This is primary corpus research, not a review or meta-analysis; the null synthesis counts and empty pooled-estimate list are appropriate (PDF pp. 2-5, Sections 1.3 and 2).
summary: The published article contains no randomized people study; its 4820 reports represent 2000 students, and all five reported-statistic strings and the numerical one-line finding match the PDF. The design and exclusion decision are supported, but six corrections are needed to supplement metadata, assignment and eligibility coding, outcome-question labels, a figure-only claim, and data/code links.
